items.question: What has drawn you toward protecting people against the misuse of AI systems in your security research?
items.object: Protecting people against AI misuse
items.answer: For the last 10 years or so, I'd probably say I've been focusing much more on computer security, and for the last few years it's been much more about computer security of AI systems, and really mostly defending machine learning systems. But in the last few years, I think it's been increasingly important to me, visible to me, that AI systems and machine learning systems are open to misuse and abuse. So a lot of my more recent attention has been spent on understanding what that looks like and building systems to protect people against misused and even weaponized versions of AI. So yeah, that's what got me here.

items.question: How do you see your work protecting people from AI misuse as a continuation of your earlier security research?
items.object: The continuity between Ben Zhao’s earlier AI security research and his work protecting people from AI misuse
items.answer: I mean, I think, like you mentioned, I worked on examples and how to defend them for a number of years. But also, more recently, I think as early as 2017, we had a paper on what happens when you can basically fool humans by writing online product reviews that are as good as human-written ones, and people couldn't tell the difference. This was years before generative AI. Then, in 2021, we had a paper on what happens when people can mimic human speech and synthesize human speech in the voice of a particular target, and again fool humans who couldn't tell the difference. But that was also a year before generative AI got there.

items.question: How did you frame the problem you wanted to solve with your 2020 project on invasive facial recognition?
items.object: The privacy problem behind the 2020 project on invasive facial recognition
items.answer: I think it started, honestly, in 2020, when we did an early project on protecting humans against invasive facial recognition. How do you modify your own photo so that they don't get downloaded by companies like Clearview AI and then used to train models to recognize your face?
quotes: I think it started, honestly, in 2020, when we did an early project on protecting humans against invasive facial recognition.

rubrics.text: The response frames protection against invasive facial recognition as modifying one’s own photos to prevent their use in training models to recognize that person.

items.question: How do you distinguish the ugly-sweater approach to interfering with recognition classifiers from your approach to protecting people against facial recognition?
items.object: The ugly-sweater approach to interfering with recognition classifiers
items.answer: It's a little bit different. The ugly sweater thing from Tom Goin and others, for example, is more of an untargeted attack. I want to screw with your classifier.

items.question: How do you think about the way Fawkes protects someone from facial recognition?
items.object: Fawkes's approach to disrupting facial recognition
items.answer: In the Fawkes project, what we did was, facial recognition is a pretty straightforward test. There's lots of models out there; they all sort of have mutual transferability. So Fawkes basically took one of the existing models and said, okay, we're going to interpret how most models are going to see your face. We basically compute an optimization where we find the minimum set of pixels that we can alter to change your photo in such a way that it looks pretty much the same to you, but in the facial-recognition feature space you look like—I mean, make me look like Denzel Washington, right? Or someone completely different. What that does, then, is that if a model trains on this—I'm going to take all my selfies and modify them all the same way—then it's honestly going to associate the name Ben with somebody who looks like Denzel. Then somebody on the street takes a real photograph of me and sends it to the model company, they're going to come back with a blank, because the actual feature space where I should be, there's not much there, or there's lots of other people there. So it'll come back with someone else's name.

items.question: What do you see as the lasting impact of your Fawkes paper on protecting people against facial recognition?
items.object: The lasting impact of the Fawkes facial-recognition protection paper
items.answer: I think at least six or seven follow-up papers came out from different groups trying to do similar kinds of things, using slightly better models or more transferable or different approaches. I think that was the big positive: we sort of pointed people's attention to this new problem, and a lot of people jumped on it. They're still writing papers about it today. That's a plus. That's the lasting impact from that, and there are a bunch of these tools out there now that people can use.

items.question: How do you assess the feasibility of measuring what proportion of a facial recognition provider's image database has been masked?
items.object: Measuring how many images in a facial recognition provider's database have been masked
items.answer: That's a very interesting question. I never thought about it along that dimension. Difficult to know, because on an individual-photo basis, I think it's pretty challenging to figure out whether the feature-space position has been distorted or not. There are probably some techniques, but none that come to mind immediately that really work well at scale, where you can actually do this with a bunch of photos. That would be an interesting question for sure.

items.question: How did you come to understand why artists were asking whether your facial recognition protection tool Fawkes could protect their art?
items.object: Artists' request to use Fawkes to protect art from generative AI
items.answer: Last year, we had some artists reach out to us and basically say, "Hey, your tool Fawkes looks super interesting. Can it protect art?" I was utterly confused. I was like, "What do you mean? It says facial recognition. What part of that connects to art?" We wrote back this very confused email, saying, "Thank you so much for your interest, but I don't know what you mean." That was it until about three or four months later, when all the press hit about the image generators, DALL-E 2 and Midjourney. My student Sean was like, literally, we had a light-bulb moment in the lab, and he was like, "Ben, is this what we're talking about in that artist email?" We said, "Oh, maybe that's it." So we reached back. We were like, "We still have that. We get it now. Is this what you mean?" This was an artist from the Netherlands, Kim. We had that old email, and she's like, "Yeah, but if you guys don't know what's going on here, jump on the Zoom call." Sure enough, we did. We're like, "All right, we don't know what the heck is going on." We get on this call, we're 10 or 15 minutes late, and it's packed—500 or 600 people, all artists, all on a single Zoom call. Just crazy. Everybody was talking about how their life is literally upside down because of generative AI models. People found that not only had their entire life's work, their entire galleries, been downloaded, scraped, and trained on, but other people were specifically using these models to literally replicate them and then use their names as a prompt so they could draw whatever they want in the style of artist X, and artist X doesn't even know.

items.question: Why do you see AI imitation of an artist's signature style as such a devastating loss of identity?
items.object: AI imitation of artists' signature styles and identities
items.answer: I did not understand the art world, and even today, it's been a year, but I still only understand snippets of it. Their signature style is their livelihood, absolutely. They work for decades to get this stuff right. They're unique. A lot of times, you can look at one single image and be like, "Oh yeah, that's Sam Yang, or that's Carla Ortiz," something very distinctive. For them, it's devastating. I've never seen anything like it. It's not like someone saying, "Oh, I took Ben's research paper and I did a thing with it." I'm not married to that thing. It's cool, but this is literally their identity, their calling card. When somebody sees that art, they're like, "Oh yeah, that's great, Greg Rutkowski. Look at that dragon." But then someone else takes that style, literally like wearing your skin and taking your entire identity, and doing things with it that you not only can't control but sometimes don't even know. One day you discover there's this whole trove of art out there that bears your name because it's part of a prompt, but obviously it's not you. You never do it that way, and in most cases it looks like crap, like really poor imitations of your art. The emotional devastation for some of these artists is so real. Self-harm is a thing; people are depressed. It's dark. Just this past week, Kelly McKernan, one of the plaintiffs in the Stability lawsuit, and I've gotten to know her over the last year. She's one of these artists who's been attacked a lot in this dimension. One of the things that really upset her this week was that she realized when you Google her name in the image column, what comes up is not her art; it's literally an AI-generated copy of her art. When your identity has been completely subsumed by AI, that's when it really hits. Greg Rutkowski had that happen to him months ago. It's a whole level of identity theft.

items.question: How do you understand the economic damage generative AI is doing to freelance artists?
items.object: Generative AI's effect on freelance artists' livelihoods
items.answer: There are so many different kinds of artists—concept artists, illustrators, graphics artists—and they all do different things. A large majority of them work on a freelance basis. They're happy doing it; it gives them freedom of scheduling, they can pick the gigs they want, and they can support themselves well. It's largely through word of mouth: they put their galleries online of their best work, and people see it. People know about their work. "Oh, you did that album cover for Tori Amos. Oh, you did that book cover for so-and-so. Love that stuff. Can you work with me on this upcoming movie poster?" That kind of stuff. I've gotten to know so many artists who a year ago were highly successful and had no worries about supporting themselves and their family, and now are literally scraping; they're losing their life savings, just trying to hang on because all the gigs are disappearing. People are using AI to generate really cheap images. Sometimes they can do okay, but most of the time, if you have anywhere near an artist eye, you'll see so many problems with this generative art. But that's what people are doing because it's cheap, and so the gigs are drying up, the freelance jobs are disappearing. On a weekly basis, you see people announcing, "It's been a good 15 years, it's been a good 23 years, but I'm going to start driving for Uber tomorrow."

items.question: How do you see the movement for certified human-created art developing?
items.object: The movement for certified human-created art
items.answer: It's rapidly becoming a thing. We went so fast from the utter fascination of, "Wow, look at that glossy thing. That's so real, and I can't believe AI produced that," to now people look at it and they're like, "Yeah, that looks so plastic and sort of soulless."

items.question: How do you view the distinction publishers and art buyers are drawing between AI-generated art and human-created commissions?
items.object: Disclosure of AI use and misrepresentation of AI-generated art as human-created commissions
items.answer: What I'm seeing is people—whether it's the book-cover industry, people who do Wizard of the Coast fantasy books, and a lot of these publishers—now getting very specific: if you're using AI, you better tell people, and if you're using AI, you're probably not going to get one of these human gigs. So now there's a delineation. Some of these AI people who are creating AI prompts and art, quote unquote, are claiming themselves to be human artists, and they're literally scamming people. People go on Twitter and tell stories: "I paid a good commission for this, and I was promised this is human art."

items.question: How do you view magazines using AI-generated models of color in place of real representation?
items.object: Magazines replacing real models of color with AI-generated models
items.answer: Months ago, we already had cases where magazines were including people of color, models of color, and it turns out they were AI-generated. Already underrepresented, everything stacked against them, and now to be replaced by AI just because it's cheaper to do that than to find real models of color and real representation. It's all kind of gross. There's not a whole lot of good about it.

items.question: How do you see generative AI affecting existing social inequalities?
items.object: Generative AI's effect on existing social inequalities
items.answer: I think it's really exacerbating the worst of what we already had: underrepresentation, bigotry, bias, wealth inequality. All these things are getting blown up and magnified by this race to the bottom. You have this technology that's really centralized in terms of who's producing it, and there's going to be a real gap between those who can afford human things versus those who are basically going to get AI things. Some companies say, "Hey, look, it's going to be great. We're going to be able to produce AI doctors." And then you ask them, "If you had a choice, who would you take?" They'd say, "Of course, I would prefer a human doctor, but in many cases people can't afford human doctors, so let's give the people who can't afford human doctors AI doctors." That's the problem: when the AI doctors are hallucinating, when they're wrong, when they're making bogus recommendations, the argument is maybe this is better than nothing. But that's a slippery slope. It's dark. It magnifies a lot of problems that already exist.

items.question: How do you see Glaze's role in protecting artists from AI models that mimic their individual styles?
items.object: Glaze as protection against AI models that mimic individual artists
items.answer:
Glaze is really the first step. What I saw was tremendous damage to real creative people, where they were being impacted viscerally in front of them by models being fine-tuned on them. That's where you take a Stable Diffusion model and say, "I'm going to literally learn the fine-grain details of a particular person's style." When you hone in on a single person, it can get very specific very, very quick. People were training on individual artists and then sharing and even selling some of these models, like, "Would you like a Sam Yang for five bucks?" Tens of thousands of people were downloading these little mimicry models. The first thing we wanted to do was stop this. Glaze does that.

Glaze basically does what Fawkes does, except on art. It takes the style, takes your image, a digital image of an artwork, and understands what the current AI models would see when they look at this piece of art, in terms of style and composition. Then it asks, mathematically speaking, how do I compute the smallest set of changes so that it would look pretty much the same to human eyes, stylistically, artistically, whatever, but to the AI model it would look like a dramatically different artistic style? That's the question it answers every time you fit in an image. It'll take a realism charcoal portrait, for example, and produce a Jackson Pollock-like style. It makes small changes to the art. For the most part it looks pretty much the same. For some styles it's really hard to tell the difference, even blown up side by side; it's very subtle.

Artists can do this with their art and upload images online, feeling good because they know they won't be trained. If someone downloads that Glazed art and tries to train a model on it to subsume your style, they'll get it wrong. They'll get some other style that looks nothing like the original target.

items.question: How do you think about Glaze as a white-box attack on models that mimic artists?
items.object: Glaze as a white-box model-poisoning attack
items.answer: It's a poisoning attack. It's not an inference-time attack, so it's model poisoning. It is white box, but it transfers really well, particularly since Stable Diffusion is what most of these models use when they try to mimic, because it is the open-source version. You can't take DALL-E or Imagine or Midjourney and fine-tune it yourself. People use Stable Diffusion, and that's what we use to generate Glaze as well. That works fairly well. It is white box, it is fully accessible, and it transfers really well to the target because the target is also basically using the same model.

items.question: How did you approach the challenge of isolating artistic style when developing image perturbations?
items.object: Using style transfer to isolate artistic style for image perturbations
items.answer: That was mentally our biggest challenge, and I was most concerned about that. Turns out you can use style transfer to solve this problem. We take your original art, give it to a local copy of Stable Diffusion, and say, "Transfer this. Do a style transfer and give me a version of this that looks like Jackson Pollock." It'll do that, and we use that output as the training target, as the projection target, for our perturbations, so we can make it look in the feature space like that Jackson Pollock version of your art. We make small changes to the original; it still looks like the original, but in the feature space it looks like a Jackson Pollock version of that same thing that you drew. items.question: Why did you evaluate Glaze by showing artists representative examples rather than having everyone upload and test their own art?
items.object: The design of Glaze's artist user study
items.answer: That would have been too much, in terms of timing and getting everyone on the same page. What we actually did was run a representative set of a few artists everybody knew, run their art through, and say, "Here's the before and after: before the change by Glaze and after the change, for different levels, different knobs, different strengths of protection." Then we showed them the protection effects. If you don't get protected, this is what you can do with mimicry; if you get protected, this is what happens after you've had the protection. We asked lots of questions, like, "What level of perturbation are you willing to tolerate on your own art now that you can see what it does to these three or four different art styles?" People are pretty good at understanding what that looks like, and they can mentally project that onto their own pieces of art. Then we show them the output and ask, "At what level do you think this is sufficient? Is this good enough protection?" So, tons of feedback, very positive, and that went into the research paper.

items.question: What did you learn about artists' computing resources that changed how you made Glaze available?
items.object: Making Glaze accessible to artists without GPU hardware
items.answer: For months I thought, "We're going to do this tool and it's going to be for GPUs, and these artists are going to make use of this." It took me three months to realize most artists don't have anywhere near that income to buy a desktop computer to run GPUs on it. These artists are like, "I could barely afford an old tablet, and everything I do is on that old tablet. What am I going to do with their GPU app?" So we built a web service, an Amazon cloud web service that we pay for, free to artists, so they can run Glaze on their own art without having to pay for a computer or GPUs. That's been hugely popular.

items.question: Why did you find smooth digital art styles particularly challenging to protect with Glaze?
items.object: Adapting Glaze's perturbations to different art styles
items.answer: Different art styles have different reactions to this. Super-smooth gradient art styles, like anime and manga and other very digital types of art, see every tiny bit of change. We really had to work hard to make that type of art amenable to Glaze, and that meant being smarter and optimizing the algorithm so it hid the perturbations in difficult-to-see places. We had comic books being Glazed, and that's crazy because it's black-and-white ink.

items.question: How do you see Glaze's limitations as a defense against fine-tuning attacks?
items.object: Glaze's defensive scope and limitations
items.answer: I see Glaze as a purely defensive tool. It protects you from the worst of the fine-tuning attacks, but it doesn't stop the whole process.

items.question: How do you see the balance of power between AI companies and artists whose work is used for training?
items.object: The power imbalance between AI companies and artists over training data
items.answer: The problem right now is that there's this massive asymmetry in power. AI companies can do whatever they want, and the only thing available to artists is opt-outs. It's the semblance of an opt-out list: maybe you can sign here and say, "Please don't scrape me or train on my art," and pray to God that some company is going to be nice enough to listen. Even if they sign you up, there's no way to verify it, validate it, or enforce it. They can say one thing and do whatever they want, and no one will be able to tell the difference, because there's no way right now in these models to definitively show whether a particular image has been trained or not. That means all the power is in the hands of the companies. We wanted to stop that, to say companies should train on licensed data, just like everybody else, just like in music, just like in other areas. Copyright is the thing, and people invest time and energy and their entire life's work into these outputs.

items.question: How do you think about Nightshade's effect on AI models trained on artwork containing it?
items.object: Nightshade as a poison pill for AI training
items.answer: Nightshade is—best analogy is basically a poison pill. It's a poison pill you can stick into your art. It's reasonably benign by itself; a single image won't do anything to you. But if you keep taking it, then pretty soon it will cause a lot of internal confusion in these models that train on them. In the worst case, if you take a lot of it, the models can potentially collapse.

items.question: How do you explain why Nightshade can affect a model trained on an enormous dataset with so few poisoned images?
items.object: The effectiveness of small numbers of poisoned images in Nightshade
items.answer: A couple things. First of all, when you look at the size of these training datasets, this is the reason why people have not looked in this direction for a long time. They think, gosh, billions of images, hundreds of millions of images. There's no way you can approach that level in terms of poison samples to make a dent. Turns out that's not really how it works. When you look inside that training set, you ask how many of them actually describe what a cat looks like or what a dog looks like. Turns out that's a really small number, a few thousand. It's not minuscule; a few thousand is a few thousand. But now the numbers get to a scale where it's a little bit more reasonable, and now you're talking about maybe a few hundred images to start breaking things for a particular concept. Let's say we just want to make dogs look like cats. There's maybe 5,000, maybe 10,000 images labeled with dog. Turns out you don't need to make a big dent in that either, because there are ways to make training data much more attractive to the model than a normal sample of average data. Training data that looks just like everything else has minimal impact. If you give it 50 copies of the same thing, after the first 10 copies it's going to be like, "Okay, I get it. These are the features for this dog, and I'm seeing nothing new." The next 40 copies aren't going to make much of a dent. But there are ways to compute changes to samples so that they look very attractive because they offer something dramatically new and yet complementary to what the model thinks and knows about this space. Using a lot of these tricks, we can lower the number down to something like 20 to 50. That's all it takes—20 to 50 poison images for a particular concept.

items.question: How do you assess the practical threat Nightshade poses to models trained on images scraped from the internet?
items.object: Nightshade’s practical threat to models trained on scraped internet images
items.answer: In the real world, obviously it's difficult to tell exactly how the companies, or every single company, sources its data. But what we do know is that there are a few places where they go regularly for scraping data, whether it's Twitter or a few other popular websites. The key here is you don't need a whole lot. What you need is less than a hundred images concentrated on a particular label. My estimate is that people will go far above that number in actual use of something like Nightshade, and the images will go everywhere. The question comes down to whether it will hit exactly the right training spot for a particular model. Maybe not, but there will be so much of it all over the place that I think it will be very difficult to avoid any particular data source for training that does not have Nightshaded images on it. We don't know how the artists will distribute the data, where they're going to post it, or how many people are going to get into it, but there are going to be a lot of people. If you're a model trainer or owner of a large model, the dangers of bumping into these tend to grow very fast depending on how fast you're scraping data and how many different places you're scraping data. The challenge is that they're visibly invisible: to the human eye, you can't just look at something and say, "Oh, that looks shaky. We're going to remove that image." You can't tell with a human eye. Potentially, all you need is 50 images to slip in for it to convince your model to do something that's very difficult to reverse. Worse yet, there are hundreds of thousands of prompts out there, things you could prompt your model for, and if something were to break it would be super hard to tell until someone actually triggered it. By then it's usually too late.

items.question: What economic change do you want Nightshade to bring about in how AI companies acquire training images?
items.object: Nightshade’s economic goal of making licensed training images more attractive than unregulated scraping
items.answer: The argument for AI trainers is that there's going to be some risk, and that risk will continue to increase as people start to adopt this more and more. At some point there's the risk and actual damage to these models, and whether they have to pay for more screening processes—we don't know if any techniques can reliably detect these images, much less remove them. Even if there were, the cost of those techniques would have to be added onto model training, and that goes up quickly. The goal isn't to ruin companies or models. The point is to make unregulated scraping of the entire internet, this whole practice of "if it's online, it's mine," so expensive that getting licensed art and licensed images from real people and paying for it, like any other normal person would, becomes more cost-effective. That's the goal: to increase the cost of this model of getting training data so much that the company will think twice, because it will be difficult to untrain or reverse some of this poison.

items.question: How do you distinguish your assumptions about training-data curation from your understanding of what makes an image more influential during model training?
items.object: Training-data curation versus an image’s influence on a model
items.answer: We don't actually make any assumptions about how the training data is curated. I actually assume it's much more about the domain and the network, and perhaps some hand curation after that. In terms of what makes a particular image more attractive to the model and have a stronger effect, that's pure math. That's just gradients.

items.question: How do you understand the way changing a poison image can increase its influence on a model during training?
items.object: The influence of a poison image on model training
items.answer: In terms of understanding what models already look like and predicting if I make a particular change to a poison image, it will make it that much more attractive to a model because the loss will be higher and the model will prefer that particular image. It's not that it's going to not train on some other images, but when trained across all these images, this particular one has more effect.

items.question: How do you see tools like Nightshade changing the way companies protect their intellectual property?
items.object: Nightshade as a way for companies to protect intellectual property
items.answer: We didn't intend this, but I think it will potentially lead to a future where companies start to build their own barriers around their own IP by using tools like Nightshade. That's going to be interesting. This is potentially a new way of enforcing copyright into the data itself. I can imagine Getty Images would be heavily incented to use something like this.
